title: The Census, the Plague, and the Threshing Floor
summary: Stirred up against Israel, David orders Joab to count the fighting men of the nation, over Joab's objection. When the count is done, David's conscience strikes him and he confesses. Through the prophet Gad, God offers three punishments; David chooses to fall into the LORD's hands, and a plague kills seventy thousand until God stops the destroying angel at the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite. David buys the threshing floor, refusing to offer what costs him nothing, builds an altar, and the plague ends.
story: Second Samuel ends not with a triumph but with a sin, a judgment, and an altar. This chapter pairs with chapter 21: both begin with a national disaster traced to the LORD's response to a king's sin and end with God answering prayer for the land. David's reign closes the way it has often gone, with the king falling and then turning back to God in repentance. Yet the last scene looks forward. The threshing floor David buys becomes the site of an altar, and 2 Chronicles 3:1 identifies it as the place where Solomon later built the temple on Mount Moriah. So the book that began with Saul's death ends by preparing the ground, literally, for the house of God that the next book will build.
historical:
The census likely took place in the later part of David's reign, when his kingdom had reached its fullest extent. The route in verses 5-7 traces a great loop: east across the Jordan to Aroer and Gad, north through Gilead to Dan and toward Sidon and Tyre on the Phoenician coast, then down to the Negev and Beersheba in the far south. Dan to Beersheba was the traditional way of naming the whole land, north to south. The trip took nearly ten months.

The parallel account in 1 Chronicles 21 differs in several details. It says Satan (or an adversary) rose up against Israel and incited David, where 2 Samuel says the LORD stirred him up. Its totals are 1,100,000 for Israel and 470,000 for Judah rather than 800,000 and 500,000, and it records a price of six hundred shekels of gold for the whole site rather than fifty shekels of silver for the threshing floor and oxen. Some reconcile these by suggesting different things were counted or bought (the floor and oxen versus the larger area); others see the differences as signs of separate sources or of copying variation in large numbers, which is common in ancient manuscripts. Araunah was a Jebusite, one of the people who held Jerusalem before David captured it (5:6-9), which shows that Jebusites still lived and owned property there.
cultural:
Why was the census sinful? The text doesn't say directly, and interpreters have proposed several reasons. Counting fighting men was the first step toward conscription and taxation, and it could express a king's trust in military strength rather than in God. Israel belonged to the LORD, not to the king, and counting it as the king's resource may have been presumption. Exodus 30:11-16 also required a ransom payment for each person counted in a census so that no plague would come on them, and some connect that law with the plague here. Joab, not a man usually known for scruples, saw the danger at once.

A threshing floor was a flat, hard, open space, often on high ground to catch the wind, where harvested grain was beaten out and winnowed. It was a natural site for gatherings and sometimes for worship. The threshing sledges and ox yokes Araunah offers were wooden farm tools that could be burned as fuel for the sacrifice. Burnt offerings, entirely consumed on the altar, expressed dedication and atonement; peace offerings were shared meals celebrating restored fellowship with God.
literary: The chapter is a tightly built narrative in four movements: the command and the census, confession and choice, plague and mercy, and purchase and sacrifice. Its key turn is David's speech in verse 17, where for the first time in the chapter he sees the people as sheep and himself as the shepherd who is guilty, and asks that the punishment fall on him. The choice of three punishments (three years, three months, three days) is built with shrinking numbers and rising intensity. Dialogue carries the final scene, with Araunah's generous offer and David's refusal forming the chapter's memorable climax. As the closing chapter of the appendix to 2 Samuel, it balances chapter 21 and ends the whole book with an altar and answered prayer.

outline.t: David orders a census over Joab's objection
The count of the fighting men
David's confession and the three choices
The plague, the angel stopped, and David's plea
The purchase of Araunah's threshing floor and the altar

doctrines.note: David confesses before any prophet confronts him, and he takes responsibility for the people's suffering, asking that God's hand fall on him and his family. Repentance here is not only sorrow but the willingness to bear the cost.

The plague ends through an altar and sacrifices offered on the site God chooses. The chapter shows the Old Testament pattern in which judgment is turned aside by sacrifice, and it locates that pattern at the future temple site.

The LORD is said to stir David up, while Chronicles names Satan as the one who incited him. Scripture holds that God rules even over evil impulses and hostile powers without being the author of sin, and David is still held responsible for his choice.

words.note: Sut, to incite or stir up, often used for enticing someone toward something harmful. Here the LORD is its subject; in 1 Chronicles 21:1 the same verb is used with Satan as subject. The two accounts together show how the Bible can speak of God's sovereignty and a hostile agent's work in the same event.

Nacham, to be sorry or to relent. When the angel reaches Jerusalem, the LORD relents from the calamity. The word describes God changing course in response to a situation, not because he was wrong but because mercy is part of his character.

Goren, threshing floor, the open place for separating grain from chaff. This particular floor becomes the site of David's altar and later of the temple, so an ordinary farm space becomes the center of Israel's worship.

Chinnam, for nothing, without cost. David refuses to offer burnt offerings that cost him nothing. The word captures the principle that true worship involves real sacrifice, not the use of someone else's gift.

christ: The chapter ends where the temple will stand, and through the temple it points toward Jesus. It shows a king who, seeing his people struck down for his sin, asks that the punishment fall on him instead. David could not bear it for them, and the plague stopped through sacrifice at an altar. The New Testament presents Jesus, the son of David and the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11), as the one who truly takes the judgment his people deserved. These are thematic connections, not predictions in the text. David's refusal to offer what cost him nothing also finds a larger echo in the gospel, which describes a sacrifice that cost God everything (Romans 8:32).

hard.q: If the LORD stirred David up to take the census, why was David punished, and why did the people die?
hard.a: The chapter says God's anger burned against Israel and he stirred David up, which raises hard questions of justice. First Chronicles 21 retells the event and names Satan as the one who incited David, and many interpreters read the two accounts together: God permitted or used an adversary's temptation as part of a judgment already due for some unnamed sin of Israel, while David freely chose and bore responsibility for his act. Others note that ancient Hebrew often attributes everything, even what God permits, directly to God, in keeping with his total sovereignty. As for the people, the text links their suffering both to the LORD's prior anger against Israel (verse 1) and to David's sin, and it also shows God cutting the plague short in mercy. David himself protests the injustice to the sheep, and the Bible lets that protest stand. The chapter doesn't resolve every question; it holds God's sovereignty, human responsibility, and divine mercy together.

questions: David wanted to count his strength. Where are you tempted to measure your security by numbers or resources rather than by trust in God?
David asked that the punishment fall on him and his house instead of the people. What does responsible leadership look like when your choices have hurt others?
David would not offer what cost him nothing. What would costly worship or generosity look like in your life right now?
